What kinds of AI models or AI services h: Structure this in two parts: classic ML deployments (e.g. classification/regression/ranking models served via REST/gRPC on Vertex AI Endpoints, GKE, or Cloud Run) and GenAI/agentic deployments (e.g. a RAG-based assistant, a summarization service, or an LLM-backed agent). For each, be ready to name the concrete artifact format (pickle, joblib, ONNX, TensorFlow SavedModel), the serving layer (FastAPI wrapper, Vertex AI Prediction, Triton, or a managed LLM API), and who owned what - typically the platform/DevOps team owns packaging, infra, scaling, and monitoring while the data science team owns model training and evaluation. Naming at least one of each type shows breadth across traditional ML and GenAI production experience.
Have you completed the full production l: Walk through the lifecycle end to end: receiving a serialized artifact from the data science team, wrapping it in a serving layer (FastAPI/Flask endpoint or a managed platform like Vertex AI/SageMaker), containerizing it with the runtime and library versions pinned to match training, building the input feature pipeline (batch or streaming) that feeds it, deploying behind a load balancer or Vertex AI Endpoint with autoscaling, and wiring up CI/CD so a new artifact version can be validated and promoted safely. Call out the handoff contract with data science - a versioned artifact, a schema for expected input features, and an evaluation report/threshold - since that is usually the part interviewers are probing for.
When monitoring ML services, do you moni: The strong answer is both, explicitly layered: infrastructure metrics (latency, error rate, CPU/memory, replica count) tell you the service is up; data and model metrics tell you the service is still correct. Describe monitoring input feature distributions (data drift), prediction distributions (concept/prediction drift), and business/ground-truth metrics (accuracy, F1, confidence score) once labels become available, plus staleness of the features feeding the model. Emphasize that infra-only monitoring is a common gap to call out - a service can be fast, healthy, and returning wrong answers, and that's the failure mode model monitoring exists to catch.
What drift metrics or ML monitoring metr: Group these into three buckets: statistical drift metrics (population stability index/PSI, KL divergence, KS test on feature distributions comparing training vs. live traffic), performance metrics tracked over time (accuracy, precision/recall, F1, AUC, confidence-score distribution), and operational ML metrics (prediction latency, feature freshness, null/missing rate on inputs, out-of-range value counts). Mention a concrete workflow: baseline the training distribution, compute drift scores on a rolling window of production inputs, and alert when a metric crosses a threshold - tying the metric names to an actual detection loop is what separates a memorized list from real experience.
You mentioned confidence score and F1 sc: This follow-up tests whether you actually understand what you operate, not just the monitoring wrapper around it. Be ready to name the model family (e.g. gradient-boosted trees like XGBoost/LightGBM for tabular classification, a fine-tuned transformer for text classification, or a logistic regression baseline) and connect it to why those specific metrics apply - F1 for imbalanced classification, confidence score from the model's predict_proba/softmax output used for a decision threshold. If you only operated the model, it is fine to say so explicitly and pivot to what you did own (serving, scaling, monitoring, retraining pipeline) rather than guessing at internals you did not build.
Have you deployed anything into producti: If you have direct experience, describe one concrete agent: what it automates (e.g. an incident-triage agent, a runbook-executing agent, or a customer-support agent), what it is allowed to do autonomously vs. what requires human approval, and how it is deployed and monitored. If your exposure is more platform/infra-adjacent, it is fine to frame it that way - e.g. 'I've deployed the infrastructure and CI/CD for LLM-backed services and have hands-on exposure to agent frameworks in personal/POC projects' - and pivot quickly to the follow-up questions, since that is usually where the interviewer is actually probing.
What framework did you use for the agent: Know the practical differences: LangChain is the general-purpose building-block library (chains, tool wrappers, retrievers); LangGraph adds explicit state machines/graphs on top for multi-step, conditional, or cyclical agent workflows and is the current default for production agents needing reliability and resumability; CrewAI and AutoGen focus on multi-agent orchestration where several role-based agents collaborate. A strong answer names the framework, why it was chosen (e.g. LangGraph for explicit control flow and checkpointing versus a simple LangChain chain for a linear RAG pipeline), and one concrete pain point encountered (e.g. debugging non-deterministic tool-call loops).
Which LLM did you use? (Vertex AI Gemini: Name the model and justify the choice on production-relevant axes: latency and cost (smaller/faster models for high-volume steps), reasoning quality (larger models for planning/tool-selection steps), data residency/compliance (a cloud-hosted model when data must stay in a specific region or VPC), and self-hosting needs (an open-weight model behind vLLM/TGI when full control or no external API dependency is required). Strong answers often mention using different models for different steps in the same agent (a cheap model for simple extraction, a stronger model for planning) rather than one model for everything.
How did the agent call tools?: Describe the tool-calling contract concretely: tools are defined with a name, a JSON-schema description of arguments, and a function/API call behind them; the LLM is given the tool schemas and returns a structured tool-call request (function name plus arguments) instead of free text; the orchestration layer validates the arguments against the schema, executes the underlying function or API call, and feeds the result back into the conversation/state for the next reasoning step. Call out validation and error handling - what happens when the LLM requests a malformed tool call or a tool call fails - since that is usually the real production concern behind this question.
How did you implement authentication and: Separate two layers: authenticating the agent itself when it calls internal services or external APIs (a dedicated service account/API key with least-privilege IAM roles, short-lived tokens via workload identity on GKE, or a secrets-manager-backed credential rather than a hardcoded key), and authorizing what the agent is allowed to do on behalf of a user (scoping tool access so the agent can only call actions the requesting user is entitled to, and gating high-risk actions behind an explicit human-in-the-loop approval step). Mentioning workload identity federation and per-tool authorization scopes, not just one blanket API key, signals production-grade thinking.
How did you monitor agent executions?: Describe tracing each agent run as a structured, multi-step trace rather than a single log line: capturing the prompt, each tool call and its arguments/result, intermediate reasoning steps, token usage/cost, latency per step, and the final output, ideally with a dedicated LLM observability tool (LangSmith, Langfuse, Arize Phoenix, or a custom structured-logging pipeline into Cloud Logging/BigQuery). Add evaluation on top of tracing - sampling a percentage of runs for human or LLM-judge review, tracking task success rate, and alerting on anomalies like runaway tool-call loops, unexpected cost spikes, or a rising rate of fallback/error responses.
How did you deploy the agent on Kubernet: Package the agent service as a container (FastAPI or similar wrapping the agent framework), deploy it as a Deployment behind a Service/Ingress on GKE with resource requests/limits sized for the LLM client's memory and connection-pool needs, and use HPA on request concurrency or custom metrics (since LLM calls are I/O-bound and CPU utilization is a poor scaling signal) rather than CPU alone. Call out statefulness: if the agent uses LangGraph checkpointing or conversation memory, that state needs to live in an external store (Redis, a database, or a checkpoint backend) rather than in-pod memory, so any pod can serve any request and rolling deploys do not drop in-flight conversations.
How did you perform model versioning and: Describe a registry-based approach: every trained artifact gets a unique version (e.g. a Vertex AI Model Registry entry or an MLflow run ID) tied to its training data snapshot, code commit, and evaluation metrics, and the serving layer references a version by that ID rather than 'latest'. Deploy new versions behind a canary or shadow-traffic stage, compare live metrics against the previous version, and keep rollback as a one-step operation (repointing the endpoint/traffic split back to the last known-good version) - the same blue/green or canary discipline used for regular service deployments, just applied to model artifacts instead of application code.
How did you handle data drift?: Describe a closed loop: compute drift metrics (PSI/KL divergence on feature distributions, or prediction-distribution shift) on a rolling window of production inputs against the training baseline, set thresholds that trigger an alert rather than relying on someone noticing a dashboard, and route the alert to whoever owns retraining decisions (often a joint platform plus data science on-call). The engineering-owned part is usually the pipeline that computes and surfaces the drift signal reliably; the decision of whether to retrain, roll back, or accept the drift is typically a data science call informed by that signal.
What happened when drift was detected?: Frame this as an escalation workflow: an alert fires when a drift metric crosses its threshold, the on-call or model owner is paged with the specific metric and magnitude, and a runbook determines next steps - often a quick sanity check (did an upstream data source change schema or stop populating a field), then a decision to either retrain on more recent data, roll back to a prior model version if performance has measurably degraded, or accept the drift if it is benign (e.g. a known seasonal shift). The key detail interviewers want is that drift detection has a defined action path, not just a dashboard nobody acts on.
How did you retrain or redeploy models?: Describe this as a pipeline, not a manual step: a retraining job (Vertex AI Pipelines, Kubeflow, or an Airflow/Cloud Composer DAG) that pulls the latest labeled data, retrains or fine-tunes the model, runs it through the same evaluation suite as the original model, and only promotes it to a candidate version if it clears defined quality gates. Redeployment then follows the same CI/CD path as any other release - build, test, canary, promote - so a retrain is just a new artifact version flowing through the existing deployment pipeline rather than a special one-off process.
What CI/CD pipeline was used for ML depl: Describe a pipeline with ML-specific gates layered on top of standard CI/CD: on artifact/code change, run unit tests plus a model-evaluation step (accuracy/F1 against a held-out test set, latency/load test on the serving container), build and push a versioned container image, deploy to a staging environment for integration testing, then promote via canary or blue/green to production with automated rollback if error rate or drift metrics regress post-deploy. Name concrete tooling if relevant - Cloud Build or Jenkins for pipeline orchestration, Vertex AI Pipelines/Kubeflow for the ML-specific steps, and ArgoCD/GKE for the actual deployment - to show this is adapted for model artifacts, not just generic CI/CD.
What was your role versus the data scien: Draw a clean boundary: the data scientist owns model selection, training, feature engineering, and offline evaluation (deciding what 'good' looks like); the platform/DevOps/MLOps engineer owns the serving infrastructure, CI/CD, containerization, scaling, security, and production monitoring (detecting when something is wrong and providing the signal, tooling, and pipeline data scientists need to act on it). Be specific about the handoff artifact (a versioned model file plus a schema and evaluation report) and where responsibilities overlap (both typically care about drift monitoring - data science defines what to measure, platform builds and operates the pipeline that measures it).
